narrative: The model estimates a 10% chance that you will fail your final year. That is a low probability, not a certainty, but it is still a warning signal, and your school is requiring remedial courses so that this remaining risk is addressed before the year ends. The three most influential factors in the model’s judgment were your past class failures, your reason for choosing this school, and your weekly study time. Importantly, all three pushed toward passing rather than failing. You have no past class failures, which was the strongest protective signal. Choosing the school for its reputation was the second strongest and also favorable. Studying five to ten hours a week was the third; this is above the most common passing-student range of two to five hours, although fewer passing students study that much, so a more consistent routine could still help. Because your headline signals are favorable, the 10% fail risk comes from smaller, less influential factors rather than from these three. To reduce it, keep attending regularly—your absences are currently zero—maintain or slightly increase your study schedule, and use the family support you already receive to check progress in weaker subjects. Treat the remedial courses as targeted practice, not as proof that you are expected to fail.
